finding.claim: reset_password_loose compares the stored reset token to the caller-supplied token with loose equality (==). If the stored token is a numeric-looking string such as '0e123...' (a magic-hash form), any other '0e...' string compares equal. If $token reaches the function as an int or bool rather than a string (for example from a JSON body, or on PHP < 8 where 0 == 'abc' is true), it can also match. The comparison also isn't constant-time. An attacker who knows the victim's email can reset the account password without the real token. The sibling reset_password uses hash_equals with a (string) cast, so this is the weaker copy.
finding.source: $email and $token arguments of reset_password_loose. The caller is not in the repo; only reset.php exists, so these presumably come from request input.
finding.sink: UPDATE users SET pw = ... WHERE email = ... at reset.php:5-6 (account password overwrite)

trace.note: Token row is loaded by the quoted email.
$row['token'] == $token uses loose comparison, so type juggling applies.
The password hash is overwritten for that email and true is returned.

finding.guards_checked: The SQL is built with $db->quote, so injection is not possible. Nothing validates the token type or format. There is no expiry check. The loose comparison is the only gate. The safe variant reset_password (lines 12-20) enforces hash_equals with a string cast. I found no callers in the repo, so reachability depends on whether the app calls the _loose variant. The finding is conditional on that.

verdict.guard_found: none on the token comparison; $db->quote() at reset.php:3,5-6 blocks SQL injection only. No type or format check on $token and no expiry check.
verdict.reason: The trace is accurate (reset.php:3-7 uses `==` at line 4 and updates the password at line 5), but exploitability depends on the unseen caller: whether $token can arrive as bool or int, and whether stored tokens can take the `0e...` form. reset.php defines no callers, so this can't be decided from the code available.
